## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Haliddirāgajātaka* (Ja 435) is a canonical Pali Jātaka tale belonging to the *Jātaka* collection [SuttaCentral]. In the commentary edited by V. Fausböll, the Buddha delivered the teaching while dwelling at Jetavana regarding a monk tempted by a coarse or plump maiden (*thullakumāripālobhana*), with the full introductory narrative referred to the *Cullanāradajātaka* in the *Terasanipāta* [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. The past story recounts a father and son living as hermits in the Himālayas; when a woman attempts to seduce the son and draw him to the city, his father admonishes him with verses on exercising discrimination in companionship and avoiding uncommitted associations [Anandajoti 2010]. In the concluding identification (*samodhāna*), the son is identified as the discontented monk, the woman as the maiden, and the father as the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1883].
Curated parallels and computational matches show substantial textual overlap with other Buddhist collections. Both SuttaCentral and DharmaNexus identify the *Araññajātaka* (Ja 348) as a primary parallel and text-reuse partner, sharing an extensive verse segment (§2.1–6.4 in Ja 435 ↔ §1.1–4.4 in Ja 348) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral also notes resembling parallels in verses from the *Brāhmaṇavagga* across multiple traditions, including *Dhammapada* 391, the Gāndhārī Dharmapada, the Patna Dharmapada, Chinese Āgama and Dharmapada translations (T 210, T 212, T 213, T 765), the Sanskrit and Tibetan *Udānavarga*, and the *Kalyāṇasīla Sutta* (Iti 97) [SuttaCentral]. Machine matches from DharmaNexus corroborate alignments with the Tibetan *Udānavarga* (D4099), the Patna Dharmapada, and the Tibetan *Nītiśāstra* (D4335), in addition to extensive Pali reuse within the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus].
The Pali text was edited in Roman characters by V. Fausböll, whose edition notes manuscript variant titles such as *Haliddhirājajātaka* and *Haliddhijātaka* [Fausböll 1883]. A selection of its verses was translated into English by Bhikkhu Ānandajoti in his anthology *Buddhist Wisdom Verses* [Anandajoti 2010].
